content:
Muslims who rise in the last part of the night to pray are often told that the practice is foreign to Jesus' religion. The Gospels say otherwise. They show Jesus rising before dawn to pray alone, praying through a whole night on a mountain, and falling on his face in prayer in the dark of Gethsemane.

The Gospels do not give the form of his prayer, and they do not show him praying the five prayers Muslims pray. What they show is the habit of night prayer, which the Quran praises in the prophets and the righteous.

This article aims to provide context to that habit, insha'Allah, in four occasions the Gospels record, each set beside the Islamic tradition of night prayer. The Quran describes the righteous in two verses: "They were in the habit of sleeping but little by night, And in the hour of early dawn, they (were found) praying for Forgiveness" (51:17 to 18).[1]

"Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there" (Mark 1:35).[2] It is the morning after a day of healing in Capernaum, when "all the city was gathered together at the door" (Mark 1:33).

The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that this hour has a special place: "Our Lord, the Blessed, the Superior, comes every night down on the nearest Heaven to us when the last third of the night remains, saying: 'Is there anyone to invoke Me, so that I may respond to invocation?'"[3] Mark's verse records prayer in the dark before dawn, which is the hour of night prayer; it is not the obligatory Fajr prayer, which begins at dawn itself.

"In these days, he went out to the mountain to pray, and he continued all night in prayer to God" (Luke 6:12).[2] The next morning he chose the Twelve. Luke places the choice after a night spent in prayer.

The Quran's command to the Prophet is the same act: "Stand (to prayer) by night, but not all night" (73:2), and "Truly the rising by night is most potent for governing (the soul), and most suitable for (framing) the Word (of Prayer and Praise)" (73:6).[1] The Prophet said: "the most excellent prayer after what is prescribed is prayer during the night."[4] The Psalms knew the same: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks to you" (Psalm 119:62).[2]

"After he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into the mountain by himself to pray. When evening had come, he was there alone" (Matthew 14:23; compare Mark 6:46).[2] It follows the feeding of the multitude. Matthew does not say how long he prayed; the next scene comes "in the fourth watch of the night".

The Quran gives the reason for such prayer in the same chapter that commands it: "True, there is for thee by day prolonged occupation with ordinary duties" (73:7), and directs the Prophet: "And pray in the small watches of the morning: (it would be) an additional prayer (or spiritual profit) for thee" (17:79).[1]

On the night of his arrest, Jesus "went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, 'My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire'" (Matthew 26:39).[2] Mark says he "fell on the ground" (Mark 14:35); Luke says he knelt (Luke 22:41).

Angela Kim Harkins reads the scene as "a reenactment of a recognizable Second Temple ritual that joined emotional prayers of supplication and confession to mourning practices".[5] The posture is the posture of sujud, and the words are submission: not my will, but yours. The Prophet said: "The nearest a servant comes to his Lord is when he is prostrating himself, so make supplication (in this state)."[6] We set out the prostration of Jesus in Jesus prostrated in prayer.

The bottom line

The Gospels record four occasions of Jesus at prayer in the dark: before dawn in a deserted place, through a whole night on a mountain, alone on a mountain at evening, and face down in Gethsemane. Luke adds that "he withdrew himself into the desert, and prayed" as a habit (Luke 5:16).[2] They do not give the form of his prayers, and they do not make them the Islamic prayers of today.

They do show the habit the Quran praises in the righteous and commands to the Prophet: rising by night to pray, seek forgiveness and submit. In the Quran, Jesus speaks of prayer as a command he was given from the cradle: "He hath ... enjoined on me Prayer and Charity as long as I live" (19:31).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 17:79; 19:31; 51:17 to 18; 73:2 to 7, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Mark 1:32 to 35; 6:46; 14:35; Luke 5:16; 6:12 to 13; 22:41; Matthew 14:23 to 25; 26:39; Psalm 119:62 (World English Bible).
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Prayer at Night (Tahajjud), the report of Abu Hurayra on the last third of the night.
  4. Sahih Muslim, Book of Fasting, the report of Abu Hurayra on the best prayer after the prescribed prayers.
  5. Angela Kim Harkins, "Ritualizing Jesus' Grief at Gethsemane", Journal for the Study of the New Testament 41, no. 2 (2018), pp. 177–203, doi:10.1177/0142064X18804433.
  6. Sahih Muslim, Book of Prayers, the report of Abu Hurayra on prostration.
